paragraphs: Rabbi Abbahu. (1) He was close to the government (Sanhedrin 14). In chapter 2 of Ketubbot, 17a, and chapter 6 of Yevamot, the maids of Caesar’s house called him “the great man of his people, leader of his nation, lamp of light,” because he was exceedingly handsome, more than Rabbi Yochanan, having a dignified facial appearance—that is, a beard—and his beauty resembled Jacob’s beauty (Bava Metzia 84; Bava Batra 58). Chagigah 14a: “A respected person”—one on whose account favor is shown to his generation; above, for example Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa; below, Rabbi Abbahu in Caesar’s house. Rashi explains: he was esteemed in the royal house, as Sanhedrin says that the maids of Caesar’s house would come out, etc. Yoma 73a: Rabbi Abbahu spoke in Rabbi Yochanan’s name, and Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi turned their faces away. (That is, Rabbi Yochanan had not said it, but they did not tell him expressly that Rabbi Yochanan had not said it.) They did so out of respect for Caesar. (He was esteemed in the royal house, as Chagigah says: “A respected person, such as Rabbi Abbahu in Caesar’s house.”) He was wealthy (Rashi, Shabbat 119a) and dealt in veils (Jerusalem Talmud, end of Hazahav). In chapter Af Al Pi, 62a, when the bathhouse floor collapsed beneath him, he saved his two servants who supported him. See Jerusalem Talmud, Beitzah, first chapter, halakhah 6; you will see that its commentator did not capture the Babylonian Talmud’s meaning. I do not presently have the Gemara of Ketubbot before me. In chapter Haro'eh he saved 101 people in the bathhouse with one limb.

(2) Kohelet Rabbah, on “It is good that you grasp this,” etc., “for one who fears God will emerge with them all”: such as Rabbi Abbahu of Caesarea, who was proficient in Scripture and Mishnah. He defeated the sectarians (first chapter of Avodah Zarah, 4; Sanhedrin 39a). He blew on the fire in honor of Shabbat (Shabbat 119a). There, on b: at the departure of Shabbat they would prepare a third-grown calf for him, and he would eat a kidney. When his son Avimi grew up he asked, “Why so much? Let us leave a kidney from Friday.” He left it, and a lion came and ate the calf intended for slaughter. Sotah 40a: he praised himself as humble, and Rabbi Abba of Akko as humbler than himself. He appointed Rabbi Abba of Akko academy head, since he was poor (see there). He lived in Caesarea and instituted the sequence tekiah–shevarim–teruah–tekiah there (Rosh Hashanah 34a). He issued a ruling in Botzra (Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Kirah). He praised his son Avimi for fulfilling the commandment of honoring father and mother; Avimi had five ordained sons (see there). He sent his son Chanina (see there) to study in Tiberias, etc., and told him, “Was it because there are no graves in Caesarea that I sent you to Tiberias?” When any Torah scholar died, he tasted nothing the entire day; Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Megallechin, halakhah 7. Before his death they showed him thirteen rivers of balsam, and he said, “I thought I had labored in vain,” etc. When he died the pillars of Caesarea wept (Mo'ed Katan 25b; Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Kol Hatzelamim).

(3) Tosafot, Bava Batra 87a: he was Rabbi Yochanan’s student. Tosafot, Arvei Pesachim 100a, likewise; in Bava Batra 87b, at the beginning of the page: “It was stated concerning it: Rabbi Abbahu said [in Rabbi Yochanan’s name]”—so it should read, as stated at the end of a, and in Chullin 110a. Rabbi Abbahu said, “Rabbi Yochanan taught me,” Gittin 44b. He recited a teaching before Rabbi Yochanan, Avodah Zarah 26, end of a; he told him, “Go teach it outside,” Shabbat 106a. He asked Rabbi Yochanan, who called him “my son” (Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of chapter 2 of Berakhot). He came to Tiberias to Rabbi Yochanan; Rabbi Yochanan saw his face shining because he had learned something new (Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Hamotzi Yayin; end of Pesachim; Shekalim, chapter 3; Midrash Kohelet on “Who is like the wise man”). He walked behind Rabbi Yochanan reciting the Shema; reaching filthy alleys, he fell silent, etc. He asked whether to finish it; he answered, etc., Rosh Hashanah, chapter 4, 34b. Bava Metzia, first chapter, 9: “This statement of Rabbi Abbahu is an invention.” After Rabbi Yochanan died he was with the court of Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi (see Yevamot 65b), and Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef, first chapter of Chullin. When Rabbi Abbahu went south he acted like Rabbi Chanina; when he went down to Tiberias he acted like Rabbi Yochanan, so as not to disagree with someone in his own locality (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, beginning of Ellu Devarim). He said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name that a man may teach his daughter Greek, for it is an adornment for her. Rabbi Shimon bar Abba heard and said, “Because Rabbi Abbahu wishes to teach his daughter Greek, he hangs it on Rabbi Yochanan.” Rabbi Abbahu heard and said, “May it come upon me if I did not hear it from Rabbi Yochanan” (Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Bameh Ishah; Pe'ah, chapter 1; end of Sotah). Responsa Rashba, section 413, 107d: “The incident of Rabbi Abbahu entering an inn and giving that woman a drink, and she became a donkey—I do not know how such an act could be permitted if he was Rabbi Yochanan’s student. Perhaps it was another man. The commentators likewise write that Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Yochanan’s student, would not do such an act.” End quotation. Our reading in chapter Arba Mitot, 67, end of b, is “Rabbi Yannai came to an inn,” etc. Rashi writes: “We read Yannai, not Rabbi Yannai, for this Yannai was not a worthy man: he practiced sorcery.”

(4) “Rabbi Abbahu scoffed at it”: Sanhedrin 3b, 40b; Shabbat 62b; Zevachim 12a. Some say he was among the savoraim who came after Rav Ashi, because of the unusual expression. But this expression also occurs among amoraim: “R.Ch. dismissed it”; R.Ch. writes so too. In chapter Asarah Yuchasin Rabbi Abbahu himself scoffs at Rabbi Yose bar Chanina’s words. That is, Yuchasin intends to refute those who say that this Rabbi Abbahu, accustomed to scoffing, is not Rabbi Yochanan’s student but one of the savoraim after Rav Ashi. He therefore says this is incorrect: Rabbi Abbahu himself—that is, the Rabbi Abbahu who was Rabbi Yochanan’s student—is described as scoffing, since he scoffed at Rabbi Yose bar Chanina, likewise Rabbi Yochanan’s student. At the end of Kamma, 117a, Rabbi Abbahu raised an objection to Rav Ashi. This too shows that Rabbi Abbahu was not among the savoraim after Rav Ashi, for Rav Ashi died in year 4180 from creation, as Sema writes in his introduction; or according to Ritva, first chapter of Avodah Zarah, in year 739 of the era of documents, which is 4187 from creation. The savoraim began in 4236; see part I of this work. Thus a long period separated Rav Ashi from the savoraim. True, the view that the scoffing Rabbi Abbahu was a savora has already been rejected, since he was Rabbi Yochanan’s student. But the Rabbi Abbahu who objected to Rav Ashi requires examination: it appears this is not Rabbi Yochanan’s student. In chronological order Rabbi Abbahu preceded Rav Ashi by much. Perhaps this is the Rabbi Abbahu whom I shall describe as living in Babylonia; or perhaps he objected to the early Rav Ashi.

(5) His colleague was Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba. Rabbi Abbahu expounded aggadah while Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba expounded halakhic teaching, and people left Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba. Rabbi Abbahu appeased him with a parable: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba’s words were pearls, his own small wares. Initially Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba would accompany him home out of respect for Caesar; that day Rabbi Abbahu accompanied Rabbi Chiyya, Sotah 40a. He said in Rabbi Elazar’s name: Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot, beginning of Nos'in; Shabbat 141, end of a; Yoma 80a; end of Chagigah; Sukkah 45, end of a. He asked Rabbi Elazar whether a second act of intercourse is permitted on Shabbat (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot). Eruvin 53b: the students asked Rabbi Ilai where Rabbi Abbahu was; he told them he had gone to the elders of the south. He sat with Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha and Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi (Ketubbot 84b). These three were ordained, as in chapter Hamevi Get, 29b; Rav Safra challenged their words (see above, Abba bar Marta). Yehoshua, brother of Dorai, asked Rabbi Abbahu. He answered, etc. Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha said to him, “I was with you when the question was put to Rabbi Avudmi of Haifa.” He replied, “I have not heard it; if you heard it, go rule accordingly” (Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Megallechin, halakhah 5). Rabbi Abbahu said, “Rabbi Yonatan ben Akhmai taught me,” etc. Rabbi Ze'ira asked him, “What was his standing?” He answered, “A great man, proficient in Mishnah.” Rabbi Chiyya of Kefar Techumin explained it before Rabbi (at the end of Terumot: before Rav), “and I appointed him a sage” (Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 2, mishnah 1).

(6) Rabbi Abba (see there); Rabbi Abba bar Zamini spoke to him; Rabbi Abba of Akko (see above); Abba bar Marta; Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya raised a contradiction to him; Rabbi Abba bar Binyamin. He said in Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa’s name (see above). In Rabbi Abbahu’s name, Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, chapter 5, mishnah 1, and chapter Haro'eh: Rabbi Abbahu in Rabbi Abbahu’s name. Avimi, his son (see above); Avimi bar Nazi; Avimi bar Tuvya in his name; Rabbi Avin in his name; Rabbi Acha asked him; Rabbi Acha bar Pappa objected to him; Rabbi Acha bar Chanilai; he said in Rabbi Acha bar Chanina’s name; Rabbi Achi in his name; Rabbi Ila; Rabbi Ilai (see above). He asked Rabbi Elazar (see above). Rabbi Elazar ben Menachem in his name (Yuchasin; I did not find it). Rabbi Ammi, his colleague; Ammi Vardinai in his name. He objected to Rav Ashi (see above). Rav Assi, his colleague. Rabbi Berekhiah said in Rabbi Abbahu’s name, Midrash Kohelet on “He has made everything beautiful in its time.” Rav Huna in his name; he said in Rabbi Huna’s name; Rav Huna bar Ika, his student; Zuga; Rabbi Zeira in his name; Rabbi Ze'ira, his son; Ze'ira asked him (Jerusalem Talmud, Beitzah, first chapter, halakhah 9). Rabbi Zerika; Rabbi Chaggai in his name; Rabbi Chizkiyah in his name. Chizkiyah bar Balyuti said to him; Rabbi Chiyya of Kefar Techumin (see above); Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, his colleague (see above); Chilfi, his grandson; Rabbi Chama son of Rabbah bar Abbahu; Rabbi Chama bar Abba in his time (I did not find it). In Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel’s name; Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa; Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi (see above); Rabbi Chanina of Sepphoris in his name; Rabbi Chanina, his son (see above); Rabbi Taifi Sumaka; Rabbi Yehudah bar Shalom. He came to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s locality. Rabbi Yochanan, his teacher, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Elyakim. In Rabbi Yonatan’s name; Rabbi Yonatan ben Akhmai taught him (see above). He said in Rabbi Yose bar Chanina’s name (Arvei Pesachim 100a; Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Arba Mitot; chapter Ha'ummanin; Midrash, beginning of the proem to Eikhah); Rabbi Abbahu scoffs at his words (see above). Rabbi Yose bar Chanan; Rabbi Yosef bar Chavu raised a contradiction to him; Yosef bar Chanun asked him; Rabbi Yaakov bar Zavda in his name; Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha (see above); Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha (see above). In Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakula’s name; Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef. Rabbi Yirmeyah objected to him (Temurah 3b), and he called Rabbi Yirmeyah “my son” (Bava Metzia 16b). Bar Yeshita, his interpreter. Rabbi Abbahu said, “Rabbi Yishmael ben Yaakov of Tyre asked Rabbi Yochanan, and I heard it.” (See Rabbi Shimon ben Yaakov of Tyre.) Rav Kohen; Rav Kahana, his student (Pesachim 52b; see Rashi there); Rabbi Misha; Nachum his attendant; Rabbi Simon; Rabbi Safra (see above). He saw Pantakaka in a dream; he prayed, and rain came. Ravin in his name; Rabbi Shmuel bar Sastrai in his name. He sat before Rabbi Yochanan and spoke in Shmuel’s name (Bava Metzia 99b). He was Rabbi Shimon bar Abba’s wedding attendant (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, chapter 2, mishnah 6; see above). Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim in his time. He said in Resh Lakish’s name: chapter Sheloshah She'akhalu, 47, end of a; Pesachim 46a; Beitzah 13a; Shabbat 127, end of b; Chullin 122b; Eruvin 31b. He said in R. Sheshet’s name. Rabbi Tachlifa bar Ma'arava before him. In Rabbi Tachlifa, his father-in-law’s name.
